title: PYSEC-2025-19
summary: Affected: PyPI: picklescan picklescan before 0.0.22 only considers standard pickle file extensions in the scope for its vulnerability scan. An attacker could craft a malicious model that uses Pickle and include a malicious pickle file with a non-standard file extension. Because the malicious pickle file inclusion is not considered as part of the scope of picklescan, the file would pass security checks and appear to be safe, when it could instead prove to be problematic.

title: PYSEC-2024-115
summary: Affected: PyPI: langchain-community A vulnerability in the GraphCypherQAChain class of langchain-ai/langchain-community version 0.2.5 allows for SQL injection through prompt injection. This vulnerability can lead to unauthorized data manipulation, data exfiltration, denial of service (DoS) by deleting all data, breaches in multi-tenant security environments, and data integrity issues. Attackers can create, update, or delete nodes and relationships without proper authorization, extract sensitive data, disrupt services, access data across different tenants, and compromise the integrity of the database.

title: GHSA-f8c7-rwf9-fmgm — Mercury: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in /api/terminals - access control bypass
summary:
Affected: PyPI: mercury ### Summary
A missing comma in `mercury_app/block_handler.py`'s `BLOCKED_PATTERNS` list causes the blocklist to fail to cover the `/api/terminals` endpoint. As a result, any unauthenticated attacker can spawn a full, interactive OS-level shell on the host running Mercury. ### Details
The blocklist in `mercury_app/block_handler.py` is defined as:
```
BLOCKED_PATTERNS = [
    # JupyterLab UI + API
    r"/lab(?!/(?:extensions/|api/settings(?:/|$)|api/translations(?:/|$)))(?:/.*)?"
    r"/api/terminals(?:/.*)?",
    r"/api/shutdown(?:/.*)?",
    r"/files(?:/.*)?",
]
```
The missing comma between the first and the second line causes Python to merge the rules, therefore the actual list that is blocked looks like this: /lab...(?:/.`*`)?/api/terminals(?:/.`*`)? (the first two lines joined together)
/api/shutdown(?:/.`*`)?
/files(?:/.`*`)? A direct request to `/api/terminals` does not match any of the 3 blocklist rules and is therefore **not blocked**, reaching Jupyter
Server's built-in terminal API, which spawns a real OS shell accessible over a WebSocket connection. No authentication, account, session or pre-existing access to Mercury is required. ### PoC
Testing was performed on a local Docker deployment (https://runmercury.com/deploy/dockerfile/), Mercury version 3.2.3, default
configuration.

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:8888/api/terminals

title: CVE-2026-111066 — AIOHTTP: File descriptor exhaustion in multipart requests
summary: Affected: aio-libs aiohttp AIOHTTP is an asynchronous HTTP client/server framework for asyncio and Python. From 2 until 3.14.4, multipart request processing can retain an unbounded number of open file descriptors. An unauthenticated attacker can consequently exhaust file descriptors with specially crafted multipart requests when a handler uses Request.post(). This issue is fixed in version 3.14.4.

title: CVE-2024-4412 — Expression Language Injection via User Input in Multiple WSO2 Products Permits Arbitrary Operations
summary: Affected: WSO2 Enterprise Integrator, WSO2 API Manager, WSO2 Open Banking IAM, WSO2 Identity Server, WSO2 Identity Server as Key Manager, WSO2 Open Banking AM, WSO2 Carbon Identity User Store Configuration UI, WSO2 Carbon Identity User Store Configuration, WSO2 Carbon Identity Recovery Management, WSO2 Carbon Identity Application Authentication Framework and 1 more The software accepts user-supplied data without sufficient validation, allowing for the injection of malicious Expression Language (EL) code. This can lead to the execution of arbitrary operations within the affected deployment. Exploitation of this vulnerability requires administrator privileges. The impact is minimal as EL usage is restricted to certain read operations.

title: CVE-2026-12350 — IBM MQ Deserialization of Untrusted Data
summary: Affected: IBM MQ Operator, IBM MQ Advanced container images IBM MQ could allow an authenticated attacker to cause a denial of service by sending a specially crafted asynchronous consume request that crashes the queue manager agent process.

title: CVE-2026-11829 — IBM MQ Buffer Overflow
summary: Affected: IBM MQ Operator, IBM MQ Advanced container images IBM MQ could allow an authenticated attacker to cause a denial of service due to improper validation of offset values in MQOPEN requests.

title: CVE-2026-111065 — AIOHTTP: Connector pool exhaustion via Max-Age overflow
summary: Affected: aio-libs aiohttp AIOHTTP is an asynchronous HTTP client/server framework for asyncio and Python. Prior to 3.14.4, Max-Age processing can overflow and skip closing a connection. An attacker can consequently exhaust the connection pool temporarily until garbage collection resolves the connections. This issue is fixed in version 3.14.4.

subject (JWT `sub` claim) specifically as an anti-hijacking discriminator —
matching the Model Context Protocol specification's documented session-hijacking
guidance (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/security_best_practices#session-hijacking).
However, the session-resume path never checks that discriminator against the
current caller's identity, so any client that obtains a session ID (its own or
another user's) can resume that session and act with it — including on
routes with per-user backend sessions. This is aggravated by the official
Helm chart shipping a literal, publicly known default seed
(`"default-insecure-seed"`) for the key that encrypts these session IDs. ## Impact An attacker who obtains (or, under the default seed, forges) another user's
`Mcp-Session-Id` value can resume that user's MCP session against the backend
MCP server(s) bound to the route — reading conversation/tool-call state and
invoking further JSON-RPC methods (e.g. `tools/call`, `resources/read`) in the
context of that other user's already-initialized backend session. On a
multi-tenant AI Gateway deployment, this crosses the exact trust boundary the
subject-embedding was added to protect. ## Location - `internal/mcpproxy/session.go` — `clientToGatewaySessionID.backendSessionIDs()`

title: GHSA-pcc4-rvhr-2pr8 — Graphify Fortran extractor: incomplete cpp #include hardening allows arbitrary host-file read/exfiltration when indexin…
summary: Affected: PyPI: graphifyy ## Summary The Fortran extractor's C-preprocessor step (`graphify/extractors/fortran.py`, `_cpp_preprocess`) applies an incomplete `#include` hardening. The `-nostdinc -I /dev/null` flags it relies on (comment "Security (F-007)") do **not** stop a capital-`F` Fortran source file from including **absolute paths** (`#include "/etc/passwd"`) or from **path-traversing out of the corpus** (`#include "../../../../home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa"`). `cpp` always searches the directory of the file being preprocessed for quoted includes and always honours absolute include paths, regardless of `-nostdinc`/`-I`. As a result, indexing an untrusted repository that contains a `.F`/`.F90`/`.F95`/`.F03`/`.F08` file reads arbitrary local files off the host and inlines their contents into the knowledge graph, which is then shipped to the LLM/agent and written to the on-disk, shareable output (`graph.json`, `GRAPH_REPORT.md`, the Obsidian wiki, HTML/SVG exports). This is the exact "corpus-side file-exfiltration vector" the F-007 comment says it is defending against; the mitigation is bypassable. ## Severity High. Arbitrary local-file read on the host, triggered by graphify's core action (indexing an untrusted folder — "turn any folder of code ... into a queryable knowledge graph"), defeating a documented security control.
